newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Duma group agrees more Russian deposits for PSAs.
newsitem.headline: Duma group agrees more Russian deposits for PSAs.

text.p: The chairman of Russia's lower house of parliament's natural resources committee said on Monday that a second list of mineral deposits had been approved by a special group looking into production sharing agreements (PSAs).
The list comprised seven reserves eligible for development under the agreements, but had yet to be presented to the State Duma lower house of parliament, he said.

"The commission has already approved a second list comprising seven deposits," Alexei Mikhailov told journalists. "But the government has not yet submitted it to the Duma to give the Duma time to take a decision on the first list."
The first deposit list, also comprising seven deposits, was passed by the Duma on Friday in its first reading. The Duma must approve the list three times before it can pass into law.

Mikhailov said he hoped the first list would pass its second and third readings in early June. The second list would probably have to wait until Duma deputies returned from their summer recess to be reviewed, which may not be until September.
"It is therefore a shame that the Duma finishes on June 20. If it were July 20, then we could have done much more," he said.
Mikhailov is a strong supporter of production sharing agreements, which allow companies developing mineral reserves to finance projects through exporting raw materials they produce.
Supporters of the agreements say they are particularly crucial to the oil industry, because they would help reverse the steep decline in Russian oil output over the past ten years.

Delays in passing a list of reserves eligible for development under the agreements, and changes to legislation to make the agreements compatible with existing Russian law are said to be holding up foreign investments worth $60 billion.

Mikhailov said deposits on the first list alone, most of which are oil and gas reserves, would attract $16.5 billion in investment, although only around $1 billion would come directly from foreign companies.
Only two deposits on the list are open to foreign investors.
But actual foreign investment would be much higher, he said.
"Of course Russian companies will use commercial credits, bank credits and international lending agencies in the projects, so foreign investment will be significantly higher," he said.

Mikhailov did not have full details of the second list of reserves, but said it included the Western Saltym oil deposit, which is being developed jointly by the Royal Dutch Shell Group and Russian companies.
He welcomed the Duma's decision to pass the first list of seven reserves on Friday, saying it would speed up the overall process of passing legislation and other reserve lists.

Conservative and nationalist opposition to the agreements in the Duma has blocked their path at almost every turn, and an original list of around 250 deposits has gradually been whittled down to a list of 26 now being studied by the committee.
"At last they (parties previously opposed to the agreements) have shown a readiness to deal with concrete questions," Mikhailov said.
He said decisions on major oil projects with foreign investors, including the giant Priobsk oil field in northern Siberia and Timan Pechora in the Far North, would have to wait until the autumn.
He said in some cases this was because foreign investors in these projects had asked for decisions on the deposits to be delayed while they sorted out differences with local authorities.
--Mike Collett-White, Moscow Newsroom +7095 941 8520
